title: Python Core & Syntax Mastery
description: Test your grasp on Python basics, mutable vs immutable types, list slicing, and operators.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following Python code?
questions.explanation: Lists in Python are mutable objects. `b = a` creates a reference to the same list in memory. Modifying `b` also modifies `a`, so `len(a)` is 4.

questions.question: What does the expression `bool([])` evaluate to in Python?
questions.explanation: An empty container (like `[]`, `{}`, `""`) is falsy in Python (`bool([]) == False`). However, `[0]` is a non-empty list containing one element `0`, which is truthy (`bool([0]) == True`).

questions.question: What is the result of `"hello"[1:4]`?
questions.explanation: Slice `[1:4]` takes characters starting at index 1 ('e') up to (but not including) index 4 ('o'). Result: 'ell'.

questions.question: Which of the following is an IMMUTABLE data type in Python?
questions.explanation: Tuples, Strings, Integers, and Floats are immutable in Python. Lists, Dictionaries, and Sets are mutable.

questions.question: What is the output of `2 ** 3 ** 2` in Python?
questions.explanation: The exponentiation operator `**` has right-to-left associativity. So `2 ** 3 ** 2` is evaluated as `2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512`.

title: Data Structures & Big-O Complexity
description: Challenge yourself on time complexity, dict lookups, sets, and algorithmic efficiency.

questions.question: What is the average time complexity of checking if a key exists in a Python dictionary?
questions.explanation: Python dictionaries are implemented using Hash Tables, offering average-case O(1) time complexity for key lookup, insertion, and deletion.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the built-in `list.sort()` (Timsort) in Python?
questions.explanation: Python uses Timsort (a hybrid of Merge Sort and Insertion Sort), which has an optimal worst and average time complexity of O(n log n) and best-case O(n) on already sorted data.

questions.question: What is the output of this set comprehension?
questions.code:
s = {x % 3 for x in range(10)}
print(sorted(list(s)))
questions.explanation: `range(10)` modulo 3 yields 0, 1, 2 repeating. Since sets only store unique elements, `s` contains `{0, 1, 2}`.

questions.question: Which data structure in Python `collections` module provides O(1) append and pop from both ends?
questions.explanation: `deque` (Double-Ended Queue) provides O(1) time complexity for appending and popping from both the left and right ends.

title: Tricky Python Quirks & Gotchas
description: Think like a senior engineer! Test your knowledge on closures, default mutable arguments, and scope.

questions.question: What will calling `f()` twice print?
questions.code:
def f(val, items=[]):
    items.append(val)
    return items

print(f(1))
print(f(2))
questions.explanation: Default argument expressions in Python are evaluated once when the function is defined, NOT each time the function is called. The list `items` is shared across calls.

questions.question: What is the output of this lambda closure inside a list comprehension?
questions.code:
funcs = [lambda x: x + i for i in range(3)]
print([f(10) for f in funcs])
questions.explanation: Python lambdas capture variables by reference (late binding). When the lambdas are called, `i` has reached its final value of 2. So `10 + 2 = 12` for each function.

questions.question: What is the output of `is` comparison between small vs large integers in CPython?
questions.code:
a = 256; b = 256
c = 300; d = 300
print(a is b, c is d)
questions.explanation: CPython pre-allocates and caches integers in the range [-5, 256] (integer interning). Numbers outside this range are separate objects unless compiled in the same code block.
